stops.name: Santa Ana de Trujillo, the embrace with Morillo
stops.campa: Armistice: Spain, shaken by revolution at home, treats with the republic it called rebellion. At the village of Santa Ana, on 27 November 1820, Bolívar and Pablo Morillo, the Pacifier, his fiercest enemy, who has just signed with him the treaty that regularizes the war and buries the war to the death, dismount, embrace, dine, toast until midnight and sleep under one roof. They raise a stone where they embraced. The canon offers Santa Ana as the war's one day of grace: the duel suspended, honor exchanged between executioners.
stops.quote: To the heroic constancy of the combatants of both armies; to their unheard-of sufferings, their valor and their virtues!
stops.quote_source: Toast at the banquet of Santa Ana, 27 November 1820, as recorded in the accounts of the interview (O'Leary; Morillo's own report)

stops.name: CAMPO DE CARABOBO, the gate of Caracas
stops.campa: The armistice dies; the armies meet on the savanna of Carabobo on 24 June 1821. Páez's llaneros and the British Legion, dying in ranks on the flank hill until the plain is won, break La Torre's army in an hour; Pedro Camejo, Negro Primero, rides back mortally hit to tell Páez he comes to say farewell because he is dead. Venezuela is free on the field where the canon stations its pantheon. Bolívar writes to the Congress that Colombia's political birth is now confirmed in blood and glory.
stops.quote: Yesterday the political birth of the Republic of Colombia was confirmed with a splendid victory.
stops.quote_source: Dispatch to the Congress of Colombia on the battle of Carabobo, 25 June 1821

stops.name: Caracas, the second homecoming
stops.campa: Five days after Carabobo the Liberator enters Caracas for the second time as its deliverer: the city thinned by war, earthquake and exile, a third of its people gone, his own houses half in ruin. The bells that rang for the boy of 1783 and the victor of 1813 ring again over rubble. He gives away confiscated estates to his soldiers, forgives, organizes, and within weeks rides west and then south, where Quito and the vision's remaining cities wait. He will see Caracas only once more in his life.

stops.name: Quito, the wreath from the balcony
stops.campa: Sucre has won Pichincha on the volcano's flank; on 16 June 1822 Bolívar enters Quito under arches and rain of flowers. From a balcony over the street a laurel crown, thrown by a beautiful quiteña, strikes the Liberator on the brow; he looks up frowning and meets the black eyes of Manuela Sáenz, who does not look away. That night at the victory ball they dance until the candles gutter. The canon marks the wound precisely: at the summit of glory, a crown thrown by the woman who will one day hold death itself off him.

stops.name: GUAYAQUIL, the interview of the two liberators
stops.campa: On 26 and 27 July 1822 the two swords of the continent meet at last: Bolívar, master of the north, receives San Martín, Protector of Peru, on the quay of Guayaquil, which Bolívar has already annexed to Colombia. They confer alone, without witnesses, behind closed doors; no protocol survives, and the canon guards the mystery jealously. What is known is the result: San Martín, the abnegated one, returns to Lima, resigns his protectorate and leaves America forever, ceding the last war entire to Bolívar. One of them had to yield; the older man yields like a stoic.
stops.quote: The Protector seemed to me very military in character, active, prompt and not at all dull... his character is frank.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Francisco de Paula Santander, Guayaquil, 29 July 1822

stops.name: CHIMBORAZO, the Delirium upon the roof of America
stops.campa: The canon places here the strangest text the Liberator ever signed: Mi delirio sobre el Chimborazo. Bolívar climbs the ice of the volcano that Humboldt could not summit, wrapped in the mantle of the rainbow, and at the top is seized by Time himself: the old god shows him the panorama of centuries, the truth of history, the smallness and greatness of the human theatre. He wakes on the ice, enormous-eyed, having seen. Vision, poem, or both, the register does not distinguish: on Chimborazo the Liberator spoke with Time and came down changed.
stops.quote: I came wrapped in the mantle of Iris, from where the mighty Orinoco pays tribute to the god of waters... A feverish delirium seized my mind; I felt as if ignited by a strange and higher fire. It was the God of Colombia possessing me.
stops.quote_source: Mi delirio sobre el Chimborazo (1822, as fixed in the Bolivarian documentary tradition)

stops.name: Lima, the dictator of Peru
stops.campa: Peru, half-freed and wholly divided, its congress and caudillos devouring one another while the Spanish viceroy holds the sierra, calls for the Liberator. On 1 September 1823 Bolívar lands at Callao and enters Lima, the City of Kings, between triumphal arches and dubious politicians. The Congress gives him supreme military authority, then dictatorship: the last republic hands itself to the foreigner because only he can finish the continent. Manuela follows him south. The last act of the vision of Casacoima begins.

stops.name: Pativilca, 'Triumph!'
stops.campa: In the coastal hamlet of Pativilca the Liberator lies almost dead: fever, ruin, Callao's garrison mutinied, Lima lost, Peru dissolving. The visitor Joaquín Mosquera finds a skeletal man in a chair against a garden wall and asks, heart failing him, what he will do now. The dying man's eyes light; the answer is one word, and the canon builds the whole doctrine of the impossible upon it. From this chair, the same week, he writes to old Rodríguez remembering Monte Sacro: the oath is still running.
stops.quote_source: Reply to Joaquín Mosquera at Pativilca, January 1824, as recorded in Mosquera's account (O'Leary, Memorias)

stops.name: JUNÍN, the battle without gunpowder
stops.campa: Risen from Pativilca, Bolívar rebuilds the army at Trujillo and reviews it on the freezing pampa of Cerro de Pasco, telling six thousand men they are about to save a world. On 6 August 1824, on the high plain of Junín, the cavalry of both empires meets at dusk with lance and saber alone, not one shot fired in the whole battle, and in three-quarters of a silent hour the royalist horse is destroyed. The Peruvian hussars of Suárez decide it and are renamed Hussars of Junín. The sierra opens; Ayacucho is four months away.
stops.quote: Soldiers! You are about to complete the greatest task that Heaven has ever entrusted to men: that of saving an entire world from slavery.
stops.quote_source: Proclamation to the united army at Cerro de Pasco, 2 August 1824

stops.name: Lima, the news of Ayacucho
stops.campa: Ordered by a jealous Congress in Bogotá to leave the army, Bolívar has handed the campaign to Sucre and returned to Lima. On 9 December 1824, on the plateau of Ayacucho, Sucre, before battle telling his men that on their efforts depends the fate of South America, destroys the last royal army and receives the viceroy's own sword. When the courier reaches Lima the Liberator reads the dispatch, casts off his coat, and cries victory through the halls of La Magdalena: the war begun on the 19th of April is over. He gives the glory wholly to Sucre.
stops.quote: The battle of Ayacucho is the summit of American glory, and the work of General Sucre.
stops.quote_source: Simón Bolívar, Resumen sucinto de la vida del general Sucre (1825)

stops.name: Cuzco, the crown of the Incas refused
stops.campa: Riding south through the liberated sierra, Bolívar enters Cuzco, navel of the old Inca world, under Inca arches of gold and flowers. The city gives him the keys and a crown of gold and diamonds; he holds it a moment, the man who despised Napoleon's bauble, and sends it to Sucre, the victor of Ayacucho, keeping nothing. He decrees land to the Indians and abolition of the cacique tributes. From Cuzco he writes to his sister the letter commanding that Hipólita, his true mother, be cared for like a queen.

stops.name: POTOSÍ, the standard on the Cerro Rico
stops.campa: On 26 October 1825 Bolívar climbs the Cerro Rico of Potosí, the silver mountain that fed the Spanish empire for three centuries, with Sucre and his staff, and on the summit plants the flags of Colombia, Peru and the Argentine, exactly as the fever of Casacoima promised eight years before across a continent. Standing on the treasury of the fallen empire he weighs all its silver against the journey from the Orinoco and finds the mountain the lighter thing. This is the geographic summit of the epic: the oath of Monte Sacro discharged upon a mountain of silver.
stops.quote: Standing upon this mass of silver called Potosí, whose immensely rich veins were for three hundred years the treasury of Spain, I esteem this opulence as nothing when I compare it with the glory of having carried victorious the standard of liberty from the burning shores of the Orinoco, to plant it here, on the peak of this mountain, whose breast is the wonder and the envy of the universe.
stops.quote_source: Speech on the summit of the Cerro Rico de Potosí, 26 October 1825
